The central question is: when a model trained on historical feature snapshots is served with features computed in real-time, are the values it sees at inference time actually the same values it would have seen at training time for that same moment? Feature stores attempt to bridge this by offering both an offline store (for batch training retrieval) and an online store (for low-latency serving), but these two stores are physically distinct systems — often a data warehouse and a Redis/DynamoDB layer — that synchronize asynchronously, meaning the online store is perpetually a lagged, potentially divergent approximation of ground truth feature history.

The concept of point-in-time correctness (PIT) is the discipline of ensuring that when you construct a training row for an event at timestamp t, you only use feature values that were actually available and known at time t — not values backfilled, late-arriving, or corrected afterward. Violations produce label leakage through future feature values, which inflates offline metrics and makes training-serving skew nearly invisible until production performance degrades. What experts worry about that beginners miss is that PIT violations are almost never caught by standard data validation pipelines, because the feature values look perfectly valid in isolation — they're real, non-null, schema-conformant values; the violation is temporal, not structural.

The deeper operational hazard is lag accumulation compounding into distribution shift: when upstream pipelines slow (backpressure, job failures, schema migrations), the online store freezes at a stale state while the model continues to serve — but the staleness is heterogeneous across feature groups, meaning some features are 10 minutes stale and others are 6 hours stale, producing a composite feature vector that never existed in training data at any single moment in time. An experienced engineer worries that the model's implicit assumption — that feature correlations are stable across the vector — breaks catastrophically under this partial-staleness regime, producing silent degradation that looks like concept drift rather than infrastructure failure.

The critical requirement is that your feedback loop latency (time from prediction to label) must be shorter than your staleness accumulation timescale, which fails for applications like fraud detection or loan default where labels arrive days to weeks later, rendering online temperature scaling useless precisely when staleness is worst.

A more robust alternative is conformal prediction with staleness-conditioned coverage guarantees (Angelopoulos & Bates, 2022): instead of outputting a calibrated probability, you output a prediction set whose coverage is guaranteed marginally over the joint distribution of feature freshness patterns — but this requires the staleness distribution at inference to be exchangeable with the staleness distribution at calibration time, an assumption that breaks during correlated pipeline failures where lag accumulates non-stationarily. This degrades gracefully because it conditions on observed staleness rather than marginalizing over unknown staleness, but it requires the feature store to timestamp each value at write time and propagate that timestamp to the serving layer, which most production feature stores (Feast, Tecton, Hopsworks) now support but few teams instrument end-to-end.

The fundamental epistemological limit is that no recalibration strategy can recover joint feature coherence — it can only correct the marginal score distribution — meaning that for models where the ranking order of predictions matters more than absolute calibration (recommendation, ad auction), staleness-induced reranking errors are irreducible without feature freshness guarantees at the infrastructure level rather than the model level.
